section_title: Why does the Gospel mention plentiful water?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized.

context_lines: John is baptizing at Aenon near Salim because there is plentiful water and people keep coming. This happens while Jesus’ ministry is growing and before John is imprisoned. The Gospel later clarifies that Jesus’ disciples perform the baptisms associated with His ministry. ([John 4:1–2](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/4.htm))

This detail belongs within John’s continuing witness to Christ. When his disciples report Jesus’ growing following, John welcomes it and says that Jesus must increase while he decreases. [Read John 3:22–30 in context](https://the-way-of-scripture.web.app/passages/john-3-22-30.html).
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readers understand this as a period when John’s work and Jesus’ growing ministry overlap, with John gladly directing attention to the Christ. The plentiful water also enters discussions about how baptism should be performed.

Where traditions differ is whether immersion is required. The Baptist Confession requires immersion for the proper administration of baptism. The Westminster Confession permits pouring or sprinkling, while the Catholic Catechism calls triple immersion the most expressive form and also recognizes pouring. These documents explain their traditions’ broader teachings; the single detail about plentiful water does not state every part of those teachings. ([Baptist Confession 29.4](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-29); [Westminster Confession 28.3](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Catechism §1239](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_one/article_1/iii_how_is_the_sacrament_of_baptism_celebrated.index.html))
god_plan_lines: John’s work prepares people to recognize the One who takes away sin and gives the Holy Spirit. His baptism belongs within that forward-looking witness. The Gospel has already distinguished his baptism with water from the work of the One he announces. ([John 1:29–34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/1.htm))

Later, Paul explains Christian baptism in relation to sharing in Christ’s death and walking in new life through His resurrection. That later explanation gives the wider picture of the new life baptism expresses; it should not erase the distinction between John’s preparatory work and the risen Christ’s completed work. ([Romans 6:3–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/6.htm))
current_position_lines: Our study Baptism reads the plentiful water in John 3:23 as support for immersion as the intended, normal practice. Its conclusion also recognizes that Scripture does not explicitly declare every other mode invalid and allows for pouring when immersion is unavailable.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Baptism: II. Why Immersion directly discusses John 3:23; VI. How Baptism Should Be Administered qualifies the normal practice with allowance for pouring.
